findings.body:
`process.env.PROCESSOR_KEY` is written into the debug log payload on every charge. That credential will land in whatever sink consumes `log.debug` (stdout, log agents, SIEM, support tooling) and can be used to replay charges against the processor.

Remove `key` from the log fields. Keep `orderId` and `ref` only — those are enough for support to correlate failures without exposing secrets.

```suggestion
  log.debug("charge context", { orderId: order.id, ref });
```

If support truly needs a privileged replay path, use a separate audited break-glass tool that never prints the raw key into application logs.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change writes the payment processor credential (`PROCESSOR_KEY`) into application logs on every successful charge.

## Why this is blocking

`log.debug("charge context", { …, key: process.env.PROCESSOR_KEY })` puts a live secret into the observability pipeline. Debug logs are routinely shipped to centralized log stores, retained for weeks/months, and readable by support and anyone with log-backend access. A credential in those systems is an exfiltration and replay risk, which matches the comment’s stated goal (“so support can replay failures”).

The previous `log.info` line already gave support the non-secret charge context (`orderId`, `ref`). That is the right surface for failure investigation; the processor key must stay out of log payloads entirely.

## Secondary note

Replacing the info-level “charge created” event with debug-only context also drops a useful operational signal unless debug logging is always on in production — but that is secondary to the secret leak.

**Recommendation:** request-changes
